newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese judge resigns in elections appeal case.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese judge resigns in elections appeal case.

text.p: The head of Lebanon's Constitutional Council offered his resignation on Thursday in a row over a series of appeals to the court against the results of last year's parliamentary elections.
"I officially announce my resignation from the presidency and membership of the (Constitutional) Council," Judge Wajdi al-Mallat said in a letter read to parliament by Speaker Nabih Berri.

He gave no reason but legal sources said Mallat was caught up in controversy over 19 appeals by losing candidates in last year's parliamentary elections who have asked the court to overturn the results.
Supporters of the pro-Syrian government swept to a huge majority in the 128-seat parliament amid widespread allegations of intimidation, manipulation and corruption.

Eighteen losing candidates asked the court to overturn the results of their contests and declare them the winners, and a 19th candidate demanded that the court overturn the entire election. All cited electoral errors or widespread abuses.
After Berri read out Mallat's letter, opposition deputy Boutros Harb told parliament:
"It is obvious that the Constitutional Council is being subjected to pressures and the issue should not be dealt with lightly. We want to know who is pressuring the council."
Zaher al-Khatib, another opposition deputy, said the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri was pressuring the court.
"I have information that the government or its head is interfering with the work of the council," he said.
"What is this talk? It is unacceptable," Hariri retorted angrily from the government benches.
Legal sources told Reuters the 10-member court was split and its members had been coming under pressure in the past two weeks from some of Lebanon's top officials.
Of the 19 appeals, the court was ready to overturn three election results, replacing the incumbent with the defeated candidate who appealed, the sources said.
These cases involved simple mistakes in vote-counting or omission of registered voters, they said.
The government was pressuring members of the court to limit its decisions to these cases, the sources said.
"This would have restricted the court to being a sort of accounting bureau only able to deal with cases involving mistakes in adding and subtracting," a lawyer told Reuters.

However, there were disagreements in the court and outside pressures on its members over three other cases in which the winners were civil servants or members of official institutions who failed to resign within the legal period prescribed before the election.

The sources said records were falsified to show the three men had resigned in time, but the court was undecided whether to rule on the cases because they would have brought criminal charges against the accused who were now sitting in parliament.

The sources said the court was also unlikely to rule in favour of more politically prominent appellants, like defeated Christian opposition leader Albert Moukheiber, because of the wide gap in the number of votes between him and the winning pro-government candidate.
"The difference in their votes was so great that the only way would be for the court to cancel the election rather than declaring the second-placed candidate the winner.
"The court is not going to do this because it would have required a very courageous interpretation of its role," a lawyer said.
